title: Tie at the Top: Sierra and Mt. SAC Split the Title in a Thrilling Finish
summary:
In a sport where every hundredth of a second counts, a tie for a championship is almost unheard of. But that's exactly what happened at the California Community College Swimming and Diving Championships, where Sierra College and Mt. San Antonio (Mt. SAC) each finished with 421 points. This marks the first tie in CCCAA men's swimming and diving history.

For the first two days, American River College held the top spot. But on the final day, both Sierra and Mt. SAC surged ahead. Sierra's depth was key: Logan Irvine won the 400 free relay to seal the tie, and also placed second in the 100 back (50.03) and split a 21.02 on the 200 free relay. Akim Kirilyuk anchored the 400 free relay in 44.93 and added a 1:39.21 on the 800 free relay. Individually, he was third in the 100 free (45.60), fourth in the 200 free (1:40.02), and sixth in the 200 IM (1:54.17).

Mt. SAC's Lincoln Jones was a powerhouse, winning the 200 back (1:46.65), finishing second in the 400 IM (3:53.82), and third in the 200 IM (1:49.59). On the final day, Mt. SAC had three swimmers in the top three of events, plus five more in the top eight. Their 400 free relay placed seventh, but it was enough to tie.

American River finished just three points behind, making it nearly a three-way tie. On the women's side, Long Beach City won comfortably with 500.5 points, over 90 ahead of Santa Barbara City College. For the men, it was a historic dead heat that no one will forget.
why_it_matters: This tie shows that in sports, victory sometimes isn't about being the only winner — two teams can share the highest honor, proving that every fractional second and every teammate's effort adds up to something historic.

background_read: The CCCAA (California Community College Athletic Association) oversees sports at over 100 two-year colleges in California, giving thousands of student-athletes a chance to compete at a high level before transferring to four-year universities.

In swimming, races are timed to hundredths of a second, so ties in individual events are rare but not unheard-of; however, a tie for an overall team championship is exceptionally unusual because it requires both teams to rack up the same number of points across many different events.

Sierra College (located in Rocklin, near Sacramento) and Mt. San Antonio College, or Mt. SAC (a large community college in Walnut, east of Los Angeles), both built powerful programs that came down to the final relay of the meet.
Until this historic dead heat, no men's team championship in CCCAA swimming and diving history had ever ended in a tie.

perspectives.description: Both Sierra and Mt. SAC can call themselves champions, which is a rare and exciting outcome that doubles the celebration. Their athletes, coaches, and fans get a story they'll tell for decades, proving that a tie can be just as dramatic as a clear win.

Some may feel a tie is unsatisfying — a championship should produce a single victor. Without a tie-breaking rule, the result can feel incomplete or like a missed opportunity for one team to claim sole ownership of the title, especially when only three points separated them from third place.

This outcome highlights how evenly matched the top teams were across a wide range of events. It reflects years of careful recruiting, training, and strategy coming to a single final relay without either side breaking ahead — a testament to the depth and balance of both programs.

The CCCAA may now consider adding tie-breaker procedures for future championships, such as using the result of the final relay or adding extra events. Coaches and athletes will likely treat every hundredth of a second even more seriously, knowing that a tie is possible and that rule changes might follow.
